The women's [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_at_the_Olympics "Marathon at the Olympics") at the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics") was held in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), France, on 11 August 2024. It was the 11th occurrence of the event at the [Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympics "Summer Olympics"). 
## Summary
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women%27s_marathon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Summary")]
The race began at 08:00 Central European Summer Time (UTC+2) with a starting temperature of approximately 19.4°C (67°F), slightly warmer than the men's marathon held the day before.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon#cite_note-2) As is typical for championship marathons, the race began with a large lead pack that gradually decreased in size as runners dropped off the pace. By 15 kilometers, 21 runners remained. There was a 428-metre (1,400 feet) hill climb over the next 3K. [Mélody Julien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9lody_Julien "Mélody Julien") of host France broke away from the lead pack, establishing a 15-meter lead near the [Palace of Versailles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Versailles "Palace of Versailles"). Approximately one hour into the race, [Jessica Stenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Stenson "Jessica Stenson") then moved into the lead. At the halfway point, following the main uphill section, the leading trio consisted of Mélody Julien, Jessica Stenson and [Dakotah Lindwurm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakotah_Popehn "Dakotah Popehn").
After passing a water station near the Palace, Lindwurm emerged off the front, but [Lonah Chemtai Salpeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonah_Chemtai_Salpeter "Lonah Chemtai Salpeter") and [Sardana Trofimova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardana_Trofimova "Sardana Trofimova"), caught up at 24K. Salpeter maintained the lead until [Tigst Assefa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigst_Assefa "Tigst Assefa") and [Peres Jepchirchir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir "Peres Jepchirchir") closed the gap within the next kilometer. Over the next 5K, the pack whittled down to 12. At about 28K, the race had its steepest climb, some of it up to a 13.5% grade. [Amane Beriso Shankule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amane_Beriso_Shankule "Amane Beriso Shankule") took the lead there, followed by a smaller pack including Assefa, [Hellen Obiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellen_Obiri "Hellen Obiri"), Salpeter, Jepchirchir, [Sharon Lokedi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharon_Lokedi "Sharon Lokedi"), [Eunice Chumba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eunice_Chumba "Eunice Chumba"), [Delvine Relin Meringor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delvine_Relin_Meringor "Delvine Relin Meringor"), and [Yuka Suzuki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuka_Suzuki "Yuka Suzuki").
On the downhill, [Sifan Hassan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sifan_Hassan "Sifan Hassan") caught up to the lead pack. Over the next 5 kilometres, the pack had reduced to 7 athletes. Meringor and Suzuki lost contact with the group over the following 5 kilometres. Going into the final 2 kilometres, Shankule fell off the pace from the lead group. Over the final sprint, Hassan took the lead, winning the gold medal three seconds ahead of silver medalist Assefa. Obiri won the bronze, 12 seconds further back.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon#cite_note-3)
Hassan's winning time of 2:22:55 set a new Olympic record, surpassing the previous record of 2:23:07 set in London in 2012. Hassan's winning margin of three seconds over a distance of greater than 26 miles (42 km) was the narrowest of any women's marathon at the Olympics. After the race, the Ethiopian team filed a protest to disqualify Hassan due to obstruction, which was rejected by the Jury of Appeal. At the post-race news conference, Tigst remarked (through a translator) "I didn’t expect at that moment it would happen. Maybe at that moment, if she didn’t push me I would have the gold."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon#cite_note-5)
A total of 91 athletes started the race, with 80 completing the course. [Kinzang Lhamo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinzang_Lhamo "Kinzang Lhamo") of Bhutan was the final finisher, completing the marathon in 3:52:59, and received widespread praise for her determination and embodiment of the Olympic spirit.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon#cite_note-6)
## Background
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women%27s_marathon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Background")]
The women's marathon has been present on the [Olympic athletics programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the Summer Olympics") since [1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics").
In its four-decade-long Olympic history since the 1984 Los Angeles Games, the women's marathon occurred on the last day of the athletics program for the first time, with the men's race scheduled a day before. According to [Tony Estanguet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Estanguet "Tony Estanguet"), the president of the [Paris 2024 organising committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Organising_Committee_for_the_2024_Olympic_and_Paralympic_Games "Paris Organising Committee for the 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games"), "We wanted to reverse the order in an ambition to more gender equality and bring women to the fore for the first time so the women's marathon will enjoy major visibility on 11 August to cap off the athletics program."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon#cite_note-7)
## Course
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women%27s_marathon&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Course")]
The marathon course began at the [Hôtel de Ville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel_de_Ville,_Paris "Hôtel de Ville, Paris") and traversed many of the host city's most iconic landmarks such as the [Eiffel Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiffel_Tower "Eiffel Tower") and the [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre "Louvre") before concluding at the [Les Invalides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Invalides "Les Invalides"). Paris officials have stated the route has taken inspiration from [la marche de femmes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_March_on_Versailles "Women's March on Versailles"). The route was characterized by significant elevation changes, totaling approximately 436 meters of ascent and 438 meters of descent, with gradients reaching up to 13.5%. Due to the elevation profile, the course has been discussed as one of the more challenging Olympic marathons.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon#cite_note-9)
